The Palermo Convention, with its recent 193rd ratification is a living sign that the international community is united in its resolve to counter the scourge of transnational organized crime in all its manifestations. We regret that an amendment has been submitted on a resolution that has been traditionally adopted by consensus and that strives to achieve a goal that unites us all, namely the goal of fighting transnational organized crime. With regard to the substance of the amendment, we wish to underline that the reference to child *********** proposed in OP.59 would be a new addition in this resolution. It is worth noting that the phrase child *********** is increasingly considered obsolete and potentially harmful and is therefore being replaced by the expression child sexual abuse material, language which was also proposed by the facilitator as a compromise. The concept of *********** suggests a consensual practice among adults which can and must not be associated with children. It diminishes the meaning of the criminal phenomenon at hand, namely the documented sexual abuse of a child for criminal purposes. In contrast, the reference to child sexual abuse material makes clear that firstly, a child was harmed, secondly, The creation, distribution, and possession of the material are crimes. We strongly encourage others to do the same. Thank you.

Thank you.

Chair, we would like to thank Italy for their facilitation and presenting what is a balanced text. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The Russian Federation supports the proposal of the United States to include in the draft resolution a provision on the prevention and combating of child ***********. This is one of the most serious and morally unacceptable forms of crimes. It grossly violates the basic rights of children and human dignity. The modern digital environment offers criminals with new opportunities to hide their actions and to scale up unlawful activities. Child *********** is. circulated through difficult to track online platforms, encrypted communications, and cross-border networks that extend the -- that go beyond the jurisdictions of a single state. So the international community needs to check this scourge, and that is not only desirable but necessary. Russia has consistently advocated for strengthening international cooperation in countering crime in its most dangerous and socially destructive forms. Chief among these are the production and circulation of child ***********. This is a crime that causes irreparable harm to children who require particular protection. In Russian legislation, in accordance with the specialized optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the production, dissemination, demonstration, storage, and sale of child *********** are criminalized. That includes their circulation using information telecommunications technologies. We are convinced that this resolution should contain clear and unambiguous provisions that clearly call for combating this heinous act. In this regard, we wish to note that the US proposal is fully in keeping with the spirit and letter of the Optional Protocol, which has 178 state parties. This is precisely why we are truly perplexed by the refusal of a number of delegations to support a similar proposal submitted by the Russian delegation during the last consultations. A reasonable question arises. Does that mean that these states are shirking their own responsibilities emanating from the aforementioned protocol? We genuinely hope that is not the case. Distinguished colleagues, fighting child *********** is not a matter of political preference. but it is a question of international commitments that have been undertaken. Today, we have the opportunity to express a unified, unambiguous position. Children must be protected, evil must be stopped, and the international community must act together. Russia calls upon all member states to support the inclusion in the resolution of clear language seeking to prevent and combat child ***********. May our solidarity make a real contribution to protecting those who cannot protect themselves. Thank you.
Thank you. Give the floor to Mexico.

Thank you, Chair. Mexico is grateful to Italy for facilitating this resolution. We commend the adoption of a more focused and digestible text that is in line with efforts to revitalize the work of this Assembly. Mexico's vote against the amendments introduced should not be interpreted as disagreement with the common purpose of combating the sexual exploitation of girls and boys. Quite to the contrary, our posture seeks to guarantee the utmost legal precision and the highest level of protection in accordance with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its optional protocol, the general observations of the committee and the best international practices on the subject. These have consistently indicated that the best expression is material that demonstrates exploitation or child sexual abuse. This term reflects that any sexual representation of a girl or a boy represents abuse and exploitation regardless of the format, medium, or intention of those producing it or distributing it. And so this terminology is fully consistent with our legal, international legal obligations as it promotes language that is focused on the victim, visibilizes violence, and ensures comprehensive protection of children at all times. Mexico is in favour of using this broader and updated terminology, as it is more conducive to the protection and full achievement of the rights of the child. Furthermore, the Convention on the Rights of the Child starts from the principle that girls and boys do not have the legal capacity, or indeed the psychological capacity, to give free and informed consent to participate in sexual acts. This is why any sexual or sexualised act that involves a child, a boy or a girl, is considered exploitation and/or sexual abuse. Amendment 59, in addition to not using the most up-to-date language, creates confusion between *********** and sexual exploitation or abuse, which has not been ascertained, and undermines the seriousness of the crime that is being committed. In terms of OP60 and that change, we are concerned that this may lead to some incongruence between the recently adopted convention against cybercrime and the convention on the rights of the child. The convention on cybercrime was carefully negotiated over many years, and this link would set an undesired precedent. I thank you.

Chair, I am honored to deliver the statement on amendment L.57 on behalf of Australia, Iceland, Liechtenstein, New Zealand, Norway, Switzerland, and my own country, Canada. The proposed revision creates the false impression that child *********** is distinct from and not itself a form of child sexual exploitation and abuse. This is inconsistent with the optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the sale of children, child prostitution, and child *********** as well as with the terminology and approach reflected in the new UN Convention on Cybercrime. Offences involving child *********** or child sexual exploitation and abuse material are both forms of child sexual exploitation and abuse and must be understood as such. The amendments therefore risk snaring the understanding that these crimes, diminishing recognition of their exploitative and abusive nature, and weakening the comprehensive protections that the international community has worked to advance. While some delegations may tolerate the coexistence of both terms in certain contexts, it is essential that child *********** never be presented in a way that suggests that it is not child sexual exploitation and abuse. Amendment L-57 creates exactly this problematic distinction. For these reasons, we voted against this amendment. We remain committed to working with all Member States to eliminate all forms of child sexual exploitation and abuse material and to strengthen our shared response to this grave violation of children's rights. We remain firmly committed to protecting children from all forms of sexual exploitation and abuse, including offenses related to child sexual exploitation and abuse material. Our shared responsibility is to uphold the highest standards of prevention, protection, and accountability, and to ensure that our responses do not inadvertently weaken the safeguards that children depend on. I thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Brazil has a model legislation on the rights of the child, the Statute of the Child and the Adolescent. Specifically regarding online sexual violence against children, a new law enacted by President Lula in January 2024 classifies bullying and cyberbullying as crimes under the penal code, amounting to heinous crimes when they result in serious injury or death. The first step in combating online sexual exploitation and abuse of children is the regulation of virtual platforms. Childhood is not a content for profit. Digital platforms have an ethical responsibility to adopt effective protection measures. No liberty, no freedom can justify crimes against children. As many delegations before us, Brazil regrets the presentation of the amendment to the resolution. During negotiations, the language was proposed and did not meet consensus. This was so because it's quite clear that in OP 59, the agreed language, all forms of child sexual exploitation and abuse, fully and clearly encompasses all cases of abuse against children, both on and offline. With regard to OP.60, the amendment suggests that the implementation of the Convention against Cybercrime could be conditioned to the obligations provided for in the Optional Protocol. Although Brazil is a party to the Protocol, to which we are fully committed, it is not appropriate that a General Assembly resolution, a non-binding document, should establish conditions for the application of a convention that is binding to its signatory parties. It is completely unclear, moreover, which provisions of the Convention could, in theory, be at odds of the commitments undertaken in the protocol. Without any prejudice to the foregoing, Brazil's vote on the amendment today should be seen as yet another public reiteration of my government's firm rejection of all forms of child sexual exploitation and abuse. I thank you.

On the one hand, it could introduce interpretations that reduce the gravity of the crime or introduce a subcategory of the pornographic industry when these are actually crimes of sexual exploitation and abuse. also indicates that digital photography, it could be asymmetrical in terms of its legal footing. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The Russian Federation reaffirms its ironclad support for combating crime in all forms and manifestations. We thank the coordinator of the Ombudsman Anti-Crime Resolution for their work and efforts to reach consensus. We welcome the fact that the text of the document reflects important provisions that were introduced upon Russia's initiative. Specifically, what is timely and significant is the inclusion of a call upon member states to step up their fight against fraud, including fraud committed through call centers. We trust that every state will take the necessary action to counter this crime and that certain countries will stop encouraging the use of call centers for fraudulent purposes. We welcome the new paragraph on countering the financial and logistics bases of criminal groups with a focus on virtual assets, digital currencies, and online platforms. We also note the principle of the sovereignty of states over their natural resources in the context of crimes that impact the environment. This is the first time that was introduced in the resolution. What is timely is the provision on the need to avoid duplicative efforts among UN entities, including in the context of technical cooperation in countering terrorism. We trust that the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime will adhere to precisely this approach. We also welcome the fact that the resolution reflects the signing of the UN Convention against Cybercrime in Hanoi in October. We encourage all states to sign and ratify as quickly as possible this document so that it can enter into force. We also see an opportunity for expanding the scope of the convention going forward by including additional protocols to it. We are also continuing to consistently adhere to terminology reflected in the Convention. The Russian Federation has been consistent in its advocacy for the use of the term "crimes committed using information and communication systems." This terminology is fully in keeping with the Hanoi Convention. We do not support the use in the text of the resolution the term "cybercrime" taken in isolation from ICT terminology, because this terminology is not aligned with the Convention and the UNGA Specialized Resolution 74/247. In any case, Cyber terminology in the resolution should impact the volume of commitments undertaken to cooperate on combating crimes committed with the use of ICT. Thank you.

Thank you.

Bismillahirrahmanirrahim. The Islamic Republic of Iran reaffirms its full support for the core objective of resolution S/20/AC.3/80/L.3, one, to strengthen the United Nations Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice Program, particularly by enhancing its technical cooperation capacity. However, we wish to place on record that our vote in favor of this resolution does not in any way imply a departure from or a waiver of our previously stated positions, reservations, or understandings with regard to this or any other resolutions, conventions, declarations, or documented reference herein. Any technical assistance under this resolution must be country driven and national demand based. Iran cannot accept one-size-fits-all model that restricts national priorities, rules, and regulations. Regarding cyber crime, Iran supports enhanced cooperation and technical assistance. We emphasize that accession to any international instrument is voluntary based on national assessment and not to be presumed by the resolution's language in OP 44 or any other operative paragraph. We register concern over certain normative references to gender-sensitive approaches in crime prevention. It's underscored that the interpretation of gender must be compatible with the cultural and social values of member states. Technical cooperation should not amount to prescriptive model that are inconsistent with member states' legal and religious frameworks. Iran welcomes support for restorative justice, alternative to imprisonment, and access to justice within the domestic penal jurisdiction as a source of any criminal justice reform. On burden sharing, we strongly support enhanced South-South, regional and triangular cooperation modalities. At the same time, we stress that such cooperation must be equitable and mutually respectful without disproportionate obligation on states such as ours. Request that our reservation be formally recorded in the Committee's report, with the understanding in place that The Islamic Republic of Iran reaffirms its readiness to cooperate constructively with UNODC and all Member States, which stand prepared to contribute to building sustainable criminal justice capacity in a way that respects sovereignty, institutional realities, and the legal tradition of Member States. Thank you.
Thank you. And I now turn the floor to the United States. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. The United States is pleased to join consensus on this resolution. We thank the Italian delegation for their work in shepherding this resolution through. The United States remains steadfast in prioritizing efforts to disrupt transnational criminal organizations that harm Americans. We are proud to have successfully incorporated language into this resolution calling for greater action to combat online scam operations in Southeast Asia. Additionally, the United States continues to lead efforts to disrupt alien smuggling networks that endanger lives and destabilize communities, and we urge Member States to implement the U.S.-sponsored resolution from the May 2025 Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, which calls for holding smugglers accountable for their crimes. We express our concern with the strategic effort by some delegations to give disproportionate attention to crimes that affect the environment in the hopes of justifying the need for a new protocol to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. We do not support a new protocol. Furthermore, the United States notes there is no internationally agreed definition of access to justice and will not support any programs or interpretations of this concept that do not align with U.S. policy. We also strongly denounce efforts by Russia, Cuba, Iran, and others to broaden the scope of cybercrime in ways that suppress freedom of expression and dissent. The United States will continue to protect fundamental freedoms. The United States will continue to oppose the Sustainable Development Goals. We also firmly support efforts to protect women from crime and violence while using clear and accurate language that centers on the needs of women and girls. Finally, let us be clear, this resolution does not prove there is sufficient political will to address the urgent threats posed by transnational criminal organizations. Where are the prosecution of top criminals and corrupt officials? Where are the concerted efforts to disrupt the criminal networks trafficking drugs that devastate our communities? The United States will continue to lead and address impunity when other governments stand idly by, including through visa restrictions, sanctions regimes, and other tools. The stakes are too high for complacency. We need partners who are willing to act, not just talk. Thank you.
Thank you. We now have the United Kingdom to be followed by the Dominican Republic and Peru. The UK, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair. While we support the overall objectives of the resolution, we'd like to reiterate our regret with the amendments to paragraph OP.59 and 60. Additionally, I'd like to highlight my delegation's concerns regarding OP.10. The existing international asset recovery framework under the convention, in particular, chapter 5 on asset recovery, already provides comprehensive framework for the end-to-end asset recovery process. This includes provisions on tracing, freezing, confiscating, and returning illicit assets, as well as the international cooperation and mutual legal assistance. The creation of new frameworks on this technical issue risks duplication and is not an effective use of resources. The focus on state parties should be on full implementation of existing obligations under the UNCAC. whether that's through the strengthening of their domestic systems or enhancing capacity building and technical assistance to other state parties. This does not require a special session and should continue to be taken forward through existing structures, including the working group on asset recovery and cost. The UK remains firmly committed to the global fight against corruption and to the recovery and return of corruptly obtained assets in line with Chapter 5. of UNCAC. We will continue to work constructively with partners through established mechanisms to ensure that commitments translate into tangible results. Thank you.
Thank you. The Dominican Republic, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair. The Dominican Republic is grateful to Italy for presenting this draft resolution entitled strengthening the United Nations crime prevention criminal justice program, in particular its technical cooperation capacity, my delegation is proud to firmly support this text. Its content reflects a broad and necessary vision in order to deal with global challenges in the area of crime, criminal justice, corruption, cybercrime, and transnational organized crime. Our country is at the heart of the Caribbean, a region that is highly exposed to transnational networks and also illicit financial flows, crimes that affect the environment, human trafficking and many other issues. This is why we have joined consensus and we have co-sponsored this resolution. I thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Transnational organized crime is an issue of growing complexity that is not just a threat to the security stability of states and democratic institutions, but it also affects the well-being and dignity of millions of people, especially the most vulnerable. Its impact represents a structural threat for democratic governance, peace, and sustainable development in many parts of the world, including Latin America and the Caribbean. For Peru, combating transnational organized crime is the highest priority for the state. It is in this spirit that we have co-sponsored the present resolution, introduced and facilitated by Italy, and we thank them for their immense work. We also support the amendment put forward by the United States because we think that it strengthens the resolution. The 15th of November was the International Day for the Prevention and Combating of all Forms of Transnational Organized Crime and also commemorated the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Palermo Convention and its protocols. And this date reminds us of the importance of redoubling our efforts in terms of tackling this scourge, which is undermining our institutions and weakening social cohesion. This threat knows no borders. The only way to tackle it effectively is through international cooperation. And the United Nations has a fundamental role in this end. And this is why Peru has been actively participating in multilateral fora on this subject and promoting intensified dialogue, especially with our neighboring countries, to the aim of strengthening practical cooperation and coordinating effective joint responses. In this same vein, we highlight the strategic role of the Regional United Nations Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean, UNLIREC, based in Peru. Its work is fundamental in strengthening and preventing and reducing the illicit trafficking of arms, one of the key illicit economies that fuels transnational organized crime, as highlighted by the Secretary General. These measures seek to dismantle criminal networks by ensuring and also ensuring effective responses that are fully coordinated with national justice systems. By way of conclusion, Chair, Peru reiterates its acknowledgement for the momentum behind this draft resolution. This is a clear sign of the collective will of States to continue taking action in a decisive and committed way against this shared global challenge. I thank you.

Thank you.

The Convention on Cybercrime aspires to provide the international community with a sound and robust legal framework to counter crimes committed through the misuse of ICTs to bring preparators to justice, and to promote the protection of children, public morals, and societies worldwide in the face of exponentially growing criminal activities in cyberspace. The Islamic Republic of Iran has consistently supported these objectives. Iran's delegation actively and constructively engaged throughout the process of elaborating this convention and accordingly signed the Cybercrime Convention in Hanoi, Vietnam. This step reflects Iran's longstanding and principled commitment to combating cybercrime, not only at the national level, where comprehensive measures have been in place for years. But now, also through strengthened multilateral cooperation, the non-signature on the convention reaffirms our readiness to work with the international community to promote a safe, secure, and responsible legal environment for all. It is, therefore, deeply regrettable that the United States, whose own record of large-scale cyber operations, extraterritorial digital surveillance, and destabilizing activities is well-documented, seeks to level accusations at other member states while refusing to acknowledge its own conduct in cyberspace. We call on all member states, including the United States, to refrain from politicizing technical processes and instead joining the collective effort to ensure that the Convention serves as indeed intended purpose, the strengthening global capacities to combat cybercrime for the benefit of all nations. Thank you.

After eight never-ending weeks of hard work, it is a great honor for Cuba to introduce for the second time the draft resolution entitled "The Right to Party." This resolution is a debt paid to the TRC Bureau, delegates, secretariat, interpreters, editors, technical staff, and room officers, whose incredible effort commitment and dedication deserve to be duly considered today, negotiated and subsequently adopted. It pays also a very special tribute to our voting machine, whose tireless effort this year should not be ignored. This is a human right based resolution deeply anchored in the universality, indivisibility and interdependence of human rights of which the right to party is an integral part. It is an effective enabler for multiple and intersecting form of fun for all 3C delegates in all their diversity. It was developed as a serious response to growing concern that the 3C workload could amount to torture or other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. Mr. Chair, for spurious purposes, a few delegations during the negotiation of this resolution attempted to take advantage of the matter of war resolution and the UN initiative to request the Cuban party to be biennialized or even triennialized. Can you imagine, dear delegates? This proposal did not receive any support in the room. It is crystal clear that the 3C Cuban party has become a shared heritage and must continue to be held on an annual basis. Cuba, as a serious and constructive penholder, has agreed to table this time a resolution which is shorter, actionable, and forward-looking. which introduces no problematic language, does not intend to waste UN resources, and carefully avoid recycling any contentious or irrelevant issues year after year. Rather, this resolution promotes an essential collective and individual human rights. Despite not being linked to international peace and security, we hope that our initiative will enjoy broad regional support and could be adopted by consensus. The draft resolution reads as follows. The Third Committee, having successfully concluded its working session, deeply concerned by the continuing deterioration of the mental health of TCC delegates, appreciating the great luncheon to be held not today by the Chair, expressing congratulations to all member states which have successfully convened recreational events during the 3C session, decides to celebrate at least two more parties on the occasion of the end of the work of the Third Committee. To welcome the decision to celebrate the African Group Party on Friday, December 5th at the Nigerian House. To welcome also the decision to hold the 3C Cuban party on Friday, December the 12th at the Cuban mission. Urge delegates of the third committee to freely exercise their inalienable right to party without discrimination of any kind and invite them to attend both diplomatic event. Strongly encourage delegate to wear diverse colors, including but not limited to burgundy or other complementary colors such as gray and green. reiterate unequivocally that the 3C Cuban party continues to be the favorite event of 3C delegates, one of the well-established parties at the United Nations, and the best place to enjoy, but not limited to, the delicious Cuba's mojitos. Dear colleagues, by supporting this noble initiative, you will be critically contributing to the full promotion, protection, respect, and fulfill of the human right to party, as well as to the full achievement of the shared goal of leaving no delegate without fun. Thank you so much.
